subtopic_detail: A fourth culture confirmed episode of vulval itch and thick discharge within twelve months
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 31 year old physiotherapist with her fourth episode this year of intense vulval itch, burning on passing urine and thick white discharge. Each previous episode was confirmed on swab and settled within days of a single antifungal capsule, then returned six to eight weeks later.

She is not pregnant, has taken no antibiotics or corticosteroids, and has had the same partner for three years. Her glycated haemoglobin last month was 33 mmol/mol and a human immunodeficiency virus test six months ago was negative. Today's high vaginal swab has grown Candida albicans, reported as sensitive to fluconazole.

data_table.Examination: Erythema and oedema of the vulva with two shallow fissures in the interlabial folds, thick adherent white discharge, no ulceration, no lichenification, no inguinal lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: High vaginal swab culture grew Candida albicans sensitive to fluconazole with no bacterial pathogen, vaginal pH 4.2, chlamydia and gonorrhoea nucleic acid tests negative, glycated haemoglobin 33 mmol/mol

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: A single fluconazole dose now and a further single dose at each recurrence
options.rationale: Treating each episode as it arises is exactly what has been happening and has produced four episodes in a year, because a single dose clears the symptomatic infection without altering the propensity to recur. Episodic treatment is the correct approach for isolated infections, not for a recurrent pattern. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care)
source_refs: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care

options.text: A single fluconazole dose now and the same treatment for her regular partner
options.rationale: This is not a sexually transmitted infection and randomised trials of treating the male partner show no reduction in recurrence for the woman, so partner treatment is reserved for a man with symptomatic balanitis. It also misses the need for a maintenance regimen. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care)
source_refs: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care

options.text: Topical nystatin pessaries nightly for fourteen days and then as required
options.rationale: Nystatin is less effective than the azoles against this organism and as required use leaves the same episodic pattern in place. Topical azoles are a reasonable alternative to oral treatment where tablets cannot be used, but the regimen rather than the route is the problem here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Oral nystatin to decolonise the bowel and a single fluconazole dose now
options.rationale: The idea that recurrence comes from a gastrointestinal reservoir was tested and abandoned, since oral nystatin does not reduce vaginal recurrence. The organism persists in the vagina at low density between episodes rather than being reintroduced from the bowel. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care)
source_refs: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care

options.text: Induction fluconazole then weekly fluconazole for six months as maintenance
options.rationale: Four or more culture confirmed episodes in twelve months defines recurrent disease, and the treatment that changes the pattern is an induction phase of three doses forty eight to seventy two hours apart followed by six months of weekly suppression, which keeps around ninety per cent of women free of symptoms while it is running. The culture confirming a fluconazole sensitive albicans species is what makes this regimen appropriate rather than a topical alternative. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care)
source_refs: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care

explanation.summary: Recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis is defined as four or more episodes in twelve months and affects around five to eight per cent of women of reproductive age. Confirming the diagnosis by culture rather than treating on symptoms alone is essential at this point, because the differential includes bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis, contact dermatitis, lichen sclerosus and vulvodynia, and because species identification matters: Candida glabrata and Candida krusei are intrinsically less susceptible to fluconazole and require boric acid pessaries or nystatin instead. Predisposing factors worth excluding are diabetes, immunosuppression, pregnancy, recent antibiotics and corticosteroid use, but most women with recurrent disease have none of them and it is better understood as an abnormal inflammatory response to normal vaginal colonisation. Treatment is an induction phase followed by six months of weekly suppression, which controls symptoms in around nine out of ten women during treatment, though roughly half relapse in the year after it stops and may need a further course. Partner treatment, bowel decolonisation and dietary sugar restriction have all been tested and do not work.
key_points: Four or more culture confirmed episodes in twelve months defines recurrent disease
Culture identifies non-albicans species that are intrinsically fluconazole resistant
Induction followed by six months of weekly suppression is the effective regimen
Around half relapse after treatment stops and may need a further course
Partner treatment and bowel decolonisation do not reduce recurrence
explanation.pearls: If the culture grows Candida glabrata rather than albicans, fluconazole will fail regardless of the regimen, and the usual next step is intravaginal boric acid 600 mg nightly for fourteen days, which is compounded rather than commercially available and is toxic if swallowed, so it must be labelled clearly and kept away from children.

subtopic_detail: A dilated non-filling left tube on hysterosalpingogram in a couple accepted for in vitro fertilisation
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 33 year old woman and her partner after three years of trying to conceive with no pregnancy. She has never been pregnant.

Her cycles are regular at twenty nine days and a mid luteal progesterone confirms ovulation, her anti-Mullerian hormone is normal for her age, and her partner's semen analysis is normal on two occasions. She had a laparoscopic appendicectomy at nineteen and was treated for chlamydia at twenty two. Her hysterosalpingogram and a follow up ultrasound are reported below. The couple have been accepted for a funded cycle of in vitro fertilisation and would like to start with the next cycle.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23 kg/m2, abdomen soft with a healed port site scar, uterus anteverted and mobile on bimanual examination, no adnexal tenderness, no nodularity in the pouch of Douglas
data_table.Investigations: Hysterosalpingogram shows free fill and spill on the right, with the left tube dilated along its length and no spill of contrast; transvaginal ultrasound confirms a 3 cm fluid filled tubular left adnexal structure with incomplete septa; both ovaries normal with an antral follicle count of 14; mid luteal progesterone 38 nmol/L; chlamydia nucleic acid test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Laparoscopic left salpingectomy before the first embryo transfer is performed
options.rationale: A fluid filled obstructed tube roughly halves implantation and live birth rates in assisted reproduction and about doubles the miscarriage rate, because the fluid refluxes into the cavity and is both mechanically and biochemically hostile to the embryo. Removing the tube, or occluding it proximally where adhesions make removal unsafe, restores pregnancy rates to those of women without the condition, and it is done before transfer rather than after a failed cycle. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Proceed directly to embryo transfer and reassess the tube only if it fails
options.rationale: Proceeding without treating the tube spends a funded cycle at roughly half the expected success rate and exposes her to a higher miscarriage risk, when the intervention that corrects it is a single day procedure. Waiting for failure means the cycle is lost before the problem is addressed. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Aspirate the hydrosalpinx under ultrasound guidance at the time of oocyte collection
options.rationale: Needle aspiration at the time of collection is easy and appealing but the fluid reaccumulates within days to weeks in most cases, so the benefit does not last through the implantation window, and it carries a risk of introducing infection into the pelvis. It is a fallback where surgery is refused or unsafe. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Prescribe doxycycline for fourteen days and repeat the imaging afterwards
options.rationale: The tubal damage here is the healed structural consequence of an infection cleared eleven years ago, and her current test is negative, so antibiotics cannot reopen a scarred and dilated tube. Antibiotic cover is used around instrumentation of the tract rather than as treatment for the damage itself. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care)
source_refs: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care

options.text: Refer for laparoscopic tubal reconstructive surgery to restore its patency
options.rationale: Opening the distal tube gives poor live birth rates when the tube is dilated and its lining destroyed, and it leaves a functionally useless conduit with a high risk of ectopic implantation and of the fluid simply reaccumulating. Reconstruction is considered only for mild disease in a woman declining assisted reproduction. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

explanation.summary: A hydrosalpinx is a distally obstructed, dilated, fluid filled fallopian tube, most often the late consequence of pelvic inflammatory disease, and in Australia chlamydia is the usual antecedent, frequently asymptomatic at the time. It matters out of proportion to its size because the accumulated fluid intermittently refluxes into the uterine cavity, where it impairs implantation both mechanically and through its inflammatory and embryotoxic content, roughly halving live birth rates in assisted reproduction and approximately doubling miscarriage. Randomised evidence supports removing the affected tube, or occluding it proximally when dense adhesions make excision hazardous, before embryo transfer, and this restores success rates to those of comparable women without the condition. Surgical technique matters because dissection close to the tube preserves the mesosalpingeal blood supply to the ovary and avoids compromising ovarian reserve, which is a genuine concern when the woman will undergo ovarian stimulation afterwards. A hydrosalpinx large enough to be visible on ultrasound, rather than only on contrast imaging, appears to have the greatest adverse effect, and is the group in which the case for surgery is strongest.
key_points: A hydrosalpinx roughly halves live birth rates and doubles miscarriage in assisted reproduction
Fluid refluxing into the cavity is mechanically and biochemically hostile to the embryo
Salpingectomy, or proximal occlusion where adhesions prevent it, precedes embryo transfer
Aspiration gives only transient benefit because the fluid reaccumulates
Careful dissection close to the tube preserves the ovarian blood supply
explanation.pearls: The tube found to be diseased at surgery also carries a risk that outlasts the fertility question: women with tubal damage have a markedly increased chance that any future pregnancy is ectopic, so an early ultrasound at around six weeks is arranged for every subsequent pregnancy, including one conceived through assisted reproduction.

subtopic_detail: A firm hyperkeratotic plaque persisting after three months of correctly applied ultrapotent corticosteroid
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 64 year old woman who has had vulval lichen sclerosus for five years, controlled on maintenance clobetasol propionate ointment with only occasional itch.

Four months ago she noticed a persistently sore spot on the left labium majus. You confirmed at the last visit that she applies the ointment daily to the affected area and she has used two 30 g tubes in three months, so quantity and technique are not the problem. The pale atrophic skin elsewhere on her vulva has improved over the same period and the itch has settled everywhere except this one area. She has had no bleeding and no discharge. Her cervical screening history is complete and negative and she has never smoked.

data_table.Examination: A 1.5 cm firm raised hyperkeratotic plaque with a central fissure on the left labium majus, unchanged since the last review, with surrounding pale atrophic skin and loss of the labia minora, no inguinal lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Swab of the fissure grew mixed skin flora with no Candida and no Staphylococcus aureus, glycated haemoglobin 36 mmol/mol, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase the steroid to twice daily and review the area in eight weeks
options.rationale: Escalating the frequency is reasonable when the whole vulva is under-treated, but she has used adequate quantities and every other area has responded, so a single focal region that has not is behaving differently from the surrounding disease. A further eight weeks of topical treatment delays a diagnosis that is time critical. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Add a topical antifungal to the steroid and review the area in eight weeks
options.rationale: Superimposed candidiasis is a genuine cause of persistent symptoms in women on long term ultrapotent steroid to the vulva, and it presents with itch, erythema and satellite lesions rather than a firm hyperkeratotic plaque, and her swab grew no Candida. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology

options.text: Start topical tacrolimus ointment and review the area in eight weeks time
options.rationale: A calcineurin inhibitor is a recognised second line agent for lichen sclerosus that fails corticosteroid, but it is relatively contraindicated in this setting because of theoretical concern about local immunosuppression in skin already at risk of squamous malignancy, and using it would suppress the signal being investigated. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists

options.text: Take a punch biopsy of the plaque and review her with the histology report
options.rationale: Any area of lichen sclerosus that fails to respond to three months of adequately applied ultrapotent corticosteroid, or that is fixed, thickened, ulcerated or eroded, must be biopsied, because differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia and squamous cell carcinoma arise on this background and can look like resistant disease. A punch biopsy taken from the thickest part of the abnormal area is the appropriate technique. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Refer for laser vaporisation of the plaque and review her after treatment
options.rationale: Ablative treatment destroys the tissue without providing histology, so an early invasive cancer would be both inadequately treated and rendered unstageable. Laser has no established role in lichen sclerosus and this option repeats the error of treating before diagnosing. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists

explanation.summary: Lichen sclerosus is a chronic inflammatory vulval condition, commonest after menopause, that produces itch, pallor, fissuring and progressive architectural loss with resorption of the labia minora and burying of the clitoris. First line treatment is an ultrapotent topical corticosteroid, applied daily for an induction period and then titrated to the lowest frequency that maintains control, with long term maintenance reducing both symptoms and, on cohort evidence, the risk of malignant progression. The lifetime risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma in women with this condition is around two to five per cent, and it arises through differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia, which is human papillomavirus independent, occurs in older women and is much more aggressive than the usual human papillomavirus related type seen in younger women. The practical rule is that any focal area which is fixed, thickened, ulcerated, eroded, bleeding or simply not responding to adequate treatment is biopsied rather than re-treated. Lifelong review is recommended, and patients are taught to self examine and to present with any new lump, ulcer or bleeding rather than waiting for a scheduled appointment.
key_points: Ultrapotent topical corticosteroid is first line, with long term maintenance
Lifetime risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma is around two to five per cent
Differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia is human papillomavirus independent and aggressive
Biopsy any area that is fixed, thickened, ulcerated or unresponsive to adequate treatment
Adequate steroid use is confirmed by quantity used, not by the prescription alone
explanation.pearls: A useful adherence check in this condition is the quantity of ointment consumed: a 30 g tube should last roughly twelve weeks on maintenance and about four weeks during induction, so a patient whose disease is uncontrolled while a single tube has lasted a year is under-treated, whereas one who has used the expected amount and still has a focal lesion needs a biopsy.

subtopic_detail: An incidental 5 cm unilocular ovarian cyst with a normal tumour marker eight years after the last period
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 58 year old woman referred after a computed tomography scan performed for renal colic showed a right ovarian cyst. Her last menstrual period was eight years ago and she has had no bleeding since.

She has no abdominal pain, no bloating, no early satiety and no change in bowel or urinary habit, and her weight is stable. No relative has had ovarian, breast, bowel or endometrial cancer. A dedicated transvaginal ultrasound has now been performed and is reported below, and her tumour marker has been measured.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender with no palpable mass and no shifting dullness, no inguinal or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, normal vulva and cervix on speculum examination
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound shows a right ovarian cyst of 5.2 cm that is unilocular and anechoic with a thin smooth wall, no solid component, no papillary projections, no internal septations and no internal vascularity on Doppler; left ovary normal; no free fluid in the pelvis; CA125 18 kIU/L (less than 35)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to a gynaecological oncology centre for laparotomy and staging
options.rationale: Referral to a specialist centre is reserved for a high risk of malignancy index or for ultrasound features suggesting malignancy, and her index is at the bottom of the scale with a completely simple cyst and a normal marker. Staging surgery for a benign simple cyst carries all the morbidity and none of the benefit. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Arrange laparoscopic oophorectomy at the local hospital within six weeks
options.rationale: Surgery is offered for symptomatic cysts, for cysts above about 5 cm that are enlarging or complex, or where the woman prefers it after discussion, and none of those apply to an asymptomatic simple cyst found incidentally. Oophorectomy also carries operative risk and is not required to make the diagnosis. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Repeat the ultrasound and the tumour marker in four to six months time
options.rationale: Simple unilocular anechoic cysts under about 5 to 10 cm in postmenopausal women carry a risk of malignancy well under one per cent, and with a normal marker the calculated risk index here is at the lowest level, so conservative surveillance is appropriate. Repeat imaging at four to six months confirms stability or resolution, and most such cysts resolve or remain unchanged. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis before any other decision
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is valuable for characterising a lesion that is indeterminate on ultrasound, particularly for distinguishing endometriomas, dermoids and fibroids, and this cyst is not indeterminate: it has every feature of a simple benign cyst. Additional imaging adds cost and anxiety without changing the plan. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Discharge her with no further imaging as the tumour marker is normal
options.rationale: The marker is normal in around half of early stage ovarian cancers and is raised in many benign conditions, so it is never used alone to exclude malignancy and is interpreted only alongside the ultrasound morphology and menopausal status. One period of surveillance to confirm stability is what makes conservative management safe. (Source: Cancer Council Australia)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia

explanation.summary: The assessment of an adnexal mass in a postmenopausal woman rests on combining ultrasound morphology, the CA125 concentration and menopausal status, conventionally through the risk of malignancy index, which multiplies an ultrasound feature score by a menopausal score by the marker value. Ultrasound features that raise concern are multilocularity, solid areas, papillary projections, bilateral lesions, ascites and intra-abdominal metastases, and a cyst with none of these scores zero. Simple unilocular anechoic cysts are common after menopause, are found in roughly one in five women on transvaginal scanning, and carry a risk of malignancy well below one per cent, so they are managed conservatively with a repeat scan rather than operated on. CA125 is unreliable in isolation because it is normal in about half of stage 1 disease and raised by endometriosis, fibroids, pelvic infection, heart failure, liver disease and any peritoneal irritation, which is why it is never used as a screening test in the general population. Referral to a gynaecological oncology centre is indicated for a high index, because operating within such a centre improves staging quality and survival.
key_points: The risk index combines ultrasound score, menopausal status and the marker value
Simple unilocular anechoic cysts carry a malignancy risk well under one per cent
CA125 is normal in about half of stage 1 disease and is never used alone
Conservative surveillance with a repeat scan at four to six months is standard
A high index warrants referral to a gynaecological oncology centre for surgery
explanation.pearls: Tell her what to come back for rather than only when: persistent bloating, early satiety, abdominal or pelvic pain and urinary urgency occurring on most days for more than a few weeks are the symptom cluster associated with ovarian cancer, and new symptoms of that kind matter more than the next scheduled scan.

Royal Australian College of General Practitioners

subtopic_detail: A request for permanent contraception from a woman of twenty six who has never been pregnant
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 26 year old electrician who asks to be referred for an operation to permanently prevent pregnancy. She has been with the same partner for four years, has never been pregnant, and says she has known since her teens that she does not want children.

She has taken the combined pill for eight years, forgets it two or three times a month and has troublesome breakthrough bleeding, and has twice used emergency contraception in the past year. She has seen two other general practitioners about this and was told each time that she would change her mind, which she found humiliating. She has no medical contraindication to any contraceptive method, her blood pressure is normal and she does not smoke. Her partner supports whatever she decides.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 112/70 mmHg with other vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, abdomen soft with no mass, no clinical evidence of anaemia
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 126 g/L (115-155), urine pregnancy test negative, cervical screening test negative for human papillomavirus twelve months ago

options.text: Refer her directly for laparoscopic tubal occlusion without further discussion
options.rationale: Referral without a comparison of the options is not respect for autonomy but an incomplete consent process, since a decision can only be informed if she knows that reversible methods match or beat the procedure for effectiveness. Referral remains entirely appropriate once that conversation has happened and she still wants it. (Source: Family Planning Australia)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia

options.text: Recommend a contraceptive implant or intrauterine device as the first option
options.rationale: Long acting reversible methods have failure rates of around 0.05 to 0.2 per cent a year, which equals or betters tubal occlusion, while avoiding a general anaesthetic and remaining reversible, and they solve the specific problem that is failing her now, which is a method requiring daily action. Recommending it is a clinical recommendation rather than a refusal: if she considers it and still wants a permanent procedure, she is referred. (Source: Family Planning Australia)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia

options.text: Decline the request and advise her to return when she is over thirty five
options.rationale: There is no age threshold for permanent contraception in Australia and a competent adult may consent to it, so refusing on age alone is paternalistic and has already driven her from two practices. Younger age and nulliparity are associated with higher rates of later regret, which is a reason to counsel carefully rather than to refuse. (Source: Family Planning Australia)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia

options.text: Recommend that her partner have a vasectomy instead of any procedure for her
options.rationale: Vasectomy is simpler, safer and cheaper than tubal occlusion and deserves discussion, but it is his decision to make in his own consultation, and a method that depends on the relationship continuing does not protect her if it ends. It cannot be recommended as her contraceptive plan. (Source: Family Planning Australia)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia

options.text: Recommend the progestogen only pill and review her bleeding in three months
options.rationale: Switching to another daily tablet ignores the reason her current method is failing, which is that she cannot reliably take a pill every day, and the progestogen only pill is less forgiving of late doses than the combined pill. It also causes irregular bleeding in a substantial proportion of users. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

explanation.summary: A request for permanent contraception from a young woman without children tests the difference between counselling and gatekeeping. A competent adult can consent to sterilisation at any age in Australia, and refusing on the basis of age or parity is not clinically defensible, yet the doctor still owes her an accurate comparison of the options before referral. The comparison genuinely favours long acting reversible methods on the numbers: the etonogestrel implant fails in roughly 0.05 per cent of users a year and intrauterine devices in about 0.1 to 0.8 per cent, against a cumulative ten year failure rate of around 1.9 per cent for tubal occlusion with the added risk that a pregnancy after the procedure is more likely to be ectopic. Regret after sterilisation is reported by around one in five women sterilised before the age of thirty compared with under one in twenty afterwards, and it is higher again after nulliparity and after a decision made around the time of a birth or a relationship change. Counselling covers permanence, the failure rate, the ectopic risk, the surgical risks and the alternatives including vasectomy, and if she still chooses the procedure after that, the referral is made without further obstruction.
key_points: A competent adult may consent to permanent contraception at any age in Australia
Implants and intrauterine devices match or beat tubal occlusion for effectiveness
Pregnancy occurring after tubal occlusion is more likely to be ectopic
Regret is higher when sterilisation occurs before thirty and after nulliparity
Counsel fully, then refer if she still chooses the procedure
explanation.pearls: If she proceeds to a tubal procedure, current Australian practice is complete removal of both tubes rather than clipping or ligation, because the distal tube is now understood to be the origin of most high grade serous ovarian cancers and salpingectomy at the time of another operation is the one accessible risk reducing step available to the general population.
